Winners & losers from F1 2026 Brazilian GP Friday practice

Aerodynamic Efficiency & Motorsport Racecraft

In premier motorsport disciplines, millisecond gains represent months of high-intensity computational fluid dynamics (CFD) research. The developments reported by The Race underline how tire degradation curves, ground-effect aero seals, and power-unit energy recovery systems dictate race outcomes. Big Picture: Upcoming grand prix telemetry and trackside upgrades will reveal which teams hold the definitive technical advantage.

A familiar name at the top of the timesheet, but not your run of the mill F1 Friday at the Brazilian Grand Prix, as one struggling frontrunner got back in the groove again while the usual kings of Friday practice produced their worst result of the season.

📌 The Core Development

Here are our winners and losers from the first day of F1 track action at Interlagos.

Charles Leclerc and Ferrari had been fastest in Friday practice at three of the past four races, going back to October’s Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, and a 6-7 FP2 result in Brazil (with Leclerc behind Lewis Hamilton) was the first time all season Ferrari has finished Friday outside the top five on the timesheet. Leclerc called it a “very, very difficult Friday” and described the feeling inside the car as “strange” and “very poor”. “We were losing in the straights, but I think the car in the corners just felt probably one of the worst Friday feelings of the season," he added. “So I think there's a lot to be found in corners, more than in the straights, where we know we have a deficit. Normally we are very fast in corners and today was not the case.” Team boss Fred Vasseur joked this was a Friday when Ferrari “have 200 kilos” of fuel inside the cars in order to flip the script, such is their usually prodigious form in free practice, but in a serious moment then admitted Ferrari has “a lot of work to do on the balance”. “The drivers, they were not happy,” he confirmed, while also saying he was “not less optimistic than last week” when Leclerc topped Friday in Mexico. “We had a couple of times a deployment issue in the lap,” Vasseur added. “We have to fine-tune everything. “On his fastest lap, he [Leclerc] lost a couple of tenths in a straight line. I would say that it’s not a drama. It’s more for you [the media] to be focused on page one [of the timing screen], but we are not. “We know that we have a lot to do on the balance. The balance was not good. The tarmac is the opposite of one week ago. It’s creating a lot of work to do and a difference compared to last week.” - Ben Anderson

🔍 Background & Sector Context

Fastest in FP1 and looking competitive on longer runs - McLaren's upgrade package for Brazil appears to be working well, with the usual caveat that Fridays don't always offer perfect insight into the order. Senior racing director Randy Singh said it's "very likely" the upgrades - led by a new front wing - will stay on the car, and Friday went "really well" for the team, while Lando Norris cautioned that the team still looks two-tenths off Kimi Antonelli's Mercedes but "pretty good" compared to the other teams.

Norris also felt gently encouraged that McLaren's new 2027-ethos front wing had begun to address the long-standing edginess of the car's balance.

🔮 Strategic Outlook & What Lies Ahead

"I don’t think we can ever judge things over just one track. But so far, for today, things have seemed a little bit more straightforward." After missing FP1, Singh says Oscar Piastri was also "immediately on the pace" - something which hasn't always happened this year - but the usual rule from recent races applies: the team needs to optimise qualifying, where its knife-edge car has let its long-run pace down all too often. - Jack Benyon

Every now and then, a lesser-known Friday driver pops up high on the timesheets in an FP1 outing, which is exactly what Gabriele Mini did on his second appearance for Alpine by setting the seventh-fastest time to head the midfield pack.
